content.greeting: Ahoy, Marcus! Today you set sail on the very first episode of your pirate adventure series. Grab your pencil, because every page holds a new challenge waiting for a sharp first mate like you.
content.packet_mission: Ahoy, first mate Marcus! Your mission today is to join my crew aboard the Salty Feather, crack the numbers of the high seas, follow a real treasure map, and find out why our ship stays afloat. Every task you finish brings us one step closer to the lost treasure of Coral Island, so hoist the sails and let's begin Episode 1!
content.packet_celebration: Shiver me feathers, Marcus, you did it! You solved treasure chest math, dug up the gold in today's reading, wrote the next chapter of our story, and built a boat that floats. Episode 1 is in the logbook, and I cannot wait to see where that second map takes us next time!
content.mascot_description: A cute cartoon green parrot standing proudly with one wing raised in a salute, wearing a tiny black pirate hat with a white skull and a little red sash, holding a brass spyglass, bright colors, simple clean lines, white background, kid-friendly illustration

activities.subject: Math
activities.title: Treasure Chest Calculations
activities.description: Practice multiplication, long division, and fractions while helping Captain Squawk count and share pirate treasure.
activities.encouragement: Marcus, every coin you count today fills Captain Squawk's treasure chest, so show those big multiplication problems who the real captain is!
activities.fun_fact: Real Spanish gold coins called doubloons were so valuable that just one could pay a sailor's wages for several weeks.
instructions: CAPTAIN SQUAWK'S QUICK CALCULATIONS: 34 x 6 = ___ || 96 divided by 4 = ___ || 23 x 14 = ___ || 852 divided by 6 = ___ || 45 x 32 = ___

WORD PROBLEMS: Captain Squawk found 12 treasure chests on Coral Island. Each chest holds 24 gold coins. How many gold coins did he find in all? || Marcus steered the Salty Feather 156 miles in 4 days. The ship sailed the same distance each day. How many miles did it sail each day? || The Salty Feather has 8 sails. Marcus raised 3 of them. What fraction of the sails is still NOT raised? || The crew found 252 silver coins and shared them equally among 7 pirates. Then each pirate gave 9 coins to Captain Squawk for parrot crackers. How many coins does each pirate have left?

DRAW & SOLVE: The deck of the Salty Feather is shaped like a rectangle that is 16 planks wide and 23 planks long. Draw a rectangle and split it into an area model: break 16 into 10 + 6 and 23 into 20 + 3. Find the area of each of the four smaller boxes, then add them together to find the total number of planks. ___ x ___ = ___
activities.answer_key: Quick Calculations: 34 x 6 = 204; 96 divided by 4 = 24; 23 x 14 = 322; 852 divided by 6 = 142; 45 x 32 = 1,440. Word Problems: 1) 12 x 24 = 288 gold coins. 2) 156 divided by 4 = 39 miles per day. 3) 5/8 of the sails are not raised. 4) 252 divided by 7 = 36 coins each, then 36 - 9 = 27 coins left for each pirate. Draw and Solve: 10 x 20 = 200, 10 x 3 = 30, 6 x 20 = 120, 6 x 3 = 18. Total: 200 + 30 + 120 + 18 = 368, so 16 x 23 = 368 planks.

activities.subject: Reading
activities.title: The Lost Treasure of Coral Island
activities.description: Read the story of Marcus and Captain Squawk's first treasure hunt, then answer questions about it.
activities.encouragement: Marcus, read like a true first mate with a spyglass, and watch closely for every clue on that treasure map!
activities.fun_fact: Real pirates almost never buried their treasure; most of them spent or shared their loot quickly, so buried treasure maps are mostly a storybook idea.
activities.passage:
Marcus stood on the deck of the Salty Feather, a wooden galleon. A galleon is a large sailing ship with tall masts. Perched on his shoulder was Captain Squawk, a bright green parrot wearing a tiny black hat.

"Welcome aboard, first mate!" squawked the captain. "Today begins our very first adventure. Somewhere out there is the lost treasure of Coral Island."

Captain Squawk dropped a rolled map into Marcus's hands. It showed a rock shaped like a skull, a tall palm tree, and a big red X. Marcus lifted a brass spyglass to his eye. A spyglass is a small telescope that makes faraway things look close. Far off on the horizon, the line where the sea meets the sky, he spotted a tiny island.

"Steer north!" Marcus called. He checked the compass, and its needle pointed straight ahead. The crew pulled the ropes, and the white sails filled with wind. Waves splashed over the bow, the front of the ship.

When they reached the island, Marcus rowed a small boat to the sandy beach. He found the skull rock right away. Then he counted twenty steps to the tallest palm tree. Captain Squawk flapped above him, pointing with one wing. "Dig there, matey!"

Marcus dug and dug until his shovel hit something hard. He pulled up a wooden chest with iron corners. Inside sat a pile of gold coins, a silver anchor necklace, and another map.

"Another map?" Marcus asked.

Captain Squawk ruffled his feathers proudly. "Every great treasure leads to the next one. That, first mate, is a clue for our next episode."

Marcus grinned. Their adventure was only beginning.
instructions: What three things were drawn on the treasure map? List all three.
The story says Marcus spotted an island on the horizon. Using clues from the story, explain what the word horizon means in your own words.
Why do you think Captain Squawk was proud instead of disappointed when Marcus found a second map inside the chest? Use details from the story to support your answer.
Draw the treasure map from the story. Include the skull rock, the palm tree, and the red X, and draw a dotted line showing the path Marcus took.
If you found a treasure chest like Marcus did, what would you hope to find inside, and why? Write 2 to 3 sentences.
activities.answer_key: 1) A rock shaped like a skull, a tall palm tree, and a big red X. 2) Answers should explain that the horizon is the line far away where the sea and the sky seem to meet. 3) Possible answer: He was proud because a second map means more adventures; he says every great treasure leads to the next one and calls it a clue for the next episode. 4) Drawings should include the skull rock, palm tree, red X, and a path from the rock to the tree. 5) Answers will vary; look for a clear wish and a reason.

activities.subject: Science
activities.title: Why Does a Pirate Ship Float?
activities.description: Build a small foil boat to explore buoyancy and discover how heavy wooden ships stay on top of the water.
activities.encouragement: Marcus, you are the ship builder of the Salty Feather today, so build a boat strong enough to carry Captain Squawk's treasure!
activities.fun_fact: Some large pirate ships weighed more than 300 tons, yet they floated because their wide hulls pushed aside a huge amount of water.
instructions: OBSERVE: Take one small square of aluminum foil and squeeze it into a tight ball. Take a second square of the same size and fold up the edges to make a flat boat shape. Gently place both in a bowl of water. Describe what happens to each one.
EXPLAIN: Both pieces of foil weigh the same amount. Why do you think the boat shape floats while the tight ball sinks or floats lower? Think about how much water each shape pushes out of the way.
PREDICT: How many pennies do you think your foil boat can carry before it sinks? Write your prediction and explain why you chose that number.

TEST AND RECORD: Add pennies to your boat one at a time, placing them carefully. Record how many pennies it held before water came in. Was your prediction too high, too low, or close? What did you notice about the boat as it got heavier?
COMPARE: Real pirate ships were made of heavy wood and carried cannons, crew, and treasure. How is your foil boat like a pirate ship? How is it different?
IMPROVE: If you were the ship builder for Captain Squawk, how would you change your boat's shape so it could carry even more treasure? Draw your new design and explain why it would work better.
activities.answer_key: 1) The flat boat floats on top of the water, while the tight ball sinks or floats much lower. 2) The boat shape spreads out and pushes aside more water. When an object pushes aside water that weighs as much as the object does, the water pushes back up and it floats. This upward push is called buoyancy. 3) Predictions will vary; look for a reason. 4) Results will vary, often between 10 and 30 pennies. The boat sinks lower in the water as it gets heavier. 5) Alike: both have a hollow shape that pushes aside water and floats. Different: real ships are wood, much bigger, have sails, and carry people. 6) Answers will vary; a strong answer mentions a wider base, taller sides, or spreading the weight evenly so the boat pushes aside more water.

content.daily_reflection: Marcus, every pirate adventure needs teamwork. Which activity today felt the most like solving a real treasure hunt, and what skill helped you finish it?
content.parent_notes: This is Marcus's first packet, launching an ongoing episode series with Captain Squawk the parrot. The math section focuses on Grade 4 skills: multiplying 2-digit numbers, long division, and an intro to fractions. The Draw and Solve problem uses an area model, which works well for visual learners. The reading passage defines new vocabulary such as galleon, spyglass, horizon, and bow right in the text. The writing prompt continues the story from the reading, so it helps to finish the reading first. The science experiment needs aluminum foil, a bowl of water, and about 30 pennies; lay down a towel for easy cleanup. Marcus may enjoy keeping his Episode 2 story to build on in future packets.
